title: How Champagne Is Made
subtitle: Every step from grape to cork, and the problem each step was invented to solve.

episodes.title: A Still Wine First
episodes.hook: Before champagne can sparkle, it has to become a quiet still wine. Its very first steps, in the vineyard and at the press, are shaped by one delicate question: how do you draw white juice from black grapes?
cards: Every champagne begins life as a still wine, without a single bubble. The sparkle comes much later, and nearly every step before it is quietly preparing the ground.
The first problem the Champenois had to solve was colour. Two of Champagne's three main grapes, Pinot Noir and Meunier, are black-skinned varieties.
Happily, the flesh of these black grapes is pale. Their colour lives in the skins, in pigments called anthocyanins, and it reaches the juice only when skin and juice linger together.
So the whole aim of the harvest is to bring the grapes to the press with their skins unbroken, giving the colour as little chance as possible to escape.
That is why grapes in Champagne are picked by hand. The region's own sources put it plainly: the bunches must reach the press whole and intact.
A harvesting machine works by shaking the vines, which loosens individual berries and can split their skins, the very thing a careful presser most wants to avoid.
At the press, the bunches go in whole, stems and all, rather than being stripped from their stems and crushed first, as the grapes for many other wines are.
The pressing itself begins soon after picking and is slow, done in stages, so that the juice runs away from the skins before it can take on colour or bitterness.
The presses are loaded in measured lots called a marc, which in Champagne means four thousand kilos of grapes. Every pressing rule is written around that unit.
From each marc, the rules allow no more than 2,550 litres of juice to become champagne. Anything pressed beyond that may not carry the name.
Those 2,550 litres are not treated as one. The first 2,050 litres are called the cuvée, and the 500 litres that follow are called the taille.
The cuvée flows first and most easily from the heart of the grape. It is usually described as the finest juice, purer and more delicate, with more acidity.
The taille comes as the pressure on the grapes rises. It tends to be fruitier and fuller, carrying a little more colour and tannin from the skins.
Neither fraction is a mistake. Many producers keep them apart and use each where it serves best, and some choose to use only the cuvée for certain wines.
You will also meet the word cuvée on labels, where it simply means a particular blend. In the press house it keeps its older and narrower meaning.
Once pressed, the juice is left to settle, and then it ferments into a still wine, which the Champenois call a vin clair, a clear wine.
A vin clair is lean and sharply acidic, as you would expect from a region this far north. That sharpness is wanted, because it will carry the wine through years of ageing.
Many producers then let the wine go through malolactic conversion, which softens its sharpest acid into a rounder one. Others prevent it, to keep every bit of freshness.
By the end of these first months, a cellar holds many separate still wines, one for each grape, village and pressing the winemaker chose to keep apart.
That separateness is deliberate. It gives the winemaker a palette to paint with, and the next step, the blending, depends on it entirely.
episodes.setup: The cellar now holds many separate still wines. Next, we meet the person who must imagine how they will taste together, years from now, once they sparkle.

episodes.title: Blending Before the Bubbles
episodes.hook: Champagne is blended while it is still a still wine, long before a single bubble exists. To see why, it helps to picture a cool northern region where no two harvests are ever quite alike.
episodes.callback: We followed the grapes from the hand-picked bunch to the vin clair, a still wine bright with acidity.
cards: Blending in Champagne is called assemblage, which simply means putting together. It happens in the months after the harvest, using the still vins clairs.
The timing matters. Once the second fermentation has begun inside the bottle, the wine can no longer be blended, so every decision about the blend is made beforehand.
The winemaker who leads this work is often called the chef de cave, the cellar master. In a grower's cellar, it may simply be the family who farm the vines.
The chef de cave tastes the vins clairs one by one, wines from different grapes, villages and pressings, and imagines how each will taste years later, once it sparkles.
That act of imagination is the heart of the craft. A sharp, quiet young wine has to be judged for the champagne it will become, not for how it tastes today.
Blending exists to solve a particular problem. Champagne's weather varies a great deal, and one harvest may be generous and ripe while the next is small or green.
A producer who makes a non-vintage champagne, one without a year on the label, wants it to taste recognisably itself, whatever the latest harvest was like.
Grapes from different villages help. Chardonnay from one slope, Pinot Noir from another and Meunier from a third each bring something, and together they balance one another.
The other great tool is time, held in the form of reserve wines: still wines kept back from earlier harvests, waiting to be drawn into future blends.
Reserve wines let a cellar master soften the character of a difficult year with the qualities of a better one, so that the house style stays steady.
They also serve as a quiet store of volume. After a small harvest, reserve wines help a producer keep making enough champagne for the people who drink it.
How much reserve wine goes into a blend varies greatly between producers and between years, and a larger share does not automatically make a better wine.
Reserve wines are usually kept apart by grape, village and year, often in tanks or casks, so that each one can be called upon precisely when it is needed.
Some producers keep a different kind of reserve, called a perpetual reserve, réserve perpétuelle in French: a single blend of many years that is never completely emptied.
Each year a portion is drawn off for the new champagne, and wine from the latest harvest is added in its place, so the reserve carries a thread of every year before.
It recalls the solera system used for sherry, though it is usually simpler, kept in fewer and larger containers. Producers value the steady character it brings.
Not every champagne is blended across years. When a harvest is especially good, a producer may make a vintage champagne, drawn from that single year.
Even then, assemblage still happens across grapes and villages, so a vintage champagne is a portrait of one year rather than an escape from blending.
When the blending is done, the separate vins clairs have become one cuvée, in that word's second sense: a finished blend, still and ready for bottling.
It is still a quiet, sharp white wine. All the drama of the bubble lies ahead, in the bottle where it will spend the rest of its life.
episodes.setup: The blend is ready, and still. Next, a little sugar and a little yeast go into the bottle with it, and the wine begins to build its pressure.

episodes.title: The Second Fermentation
episodes.hook: The bubbles in champagne are not added; they are grown, inside the very bottle you will one day open. This step solved one problem beautifully, and for a long time it created another, rather dangerous one.
episodes.callback: We watched the vins clairs become a single blend, steadied by reserve wines from earlier harvests.
cards: When the blend is ready, it is bottled together with a small, measured mixture called the liqueur de tirage. Tirage is the French word for this bottling.
The liqueur de tirage is mostly sugar dissolved in wine, with selected yeast, nutrients to help the yeast work, and often a riddling aid such as bentonite, a fine clay.
The bentonite has a job much later. It helps the spent yeast slide down the glass when the time comes to remove it, rather than clinging to the sides of the bottle.
Each bottle is then sealed, nowadays usually with a crown cap like the one on a beer bottle, and a small plastic cup, the bidule, sits inside it to catch sediment.
A few producers have returned to sealing with a cork at this stage, accepting a little more variation from bottle to bottle in return for the style they prefer.
The bottles are laid on their sides in a cool cellar, and the yeast begins a second fermentation, eating the added sugar and making a little more alcohol and carbon dioxide.
The Champenois call this the prise de mousse, the taking of the foam. With nowhere to escape, the carbon dioxide dissolves into the wine itself.
The usual dose is about twenty-four grams of sugar per litre, and a widely used rule of thumb says that about four grams per litre makes one atmosphere of pressure.
Multiply them out and you arrive at the figure the region's own teaching materials give: around six bar of pressure inside the bottle, measured at twenty degrees Celsius.
The bar and the atmosphere are close cousins as units of pressure, so you will see both used. Some producers deliberately aim a little lower, for a gentler sparkle.
That is why champagne bottles are made of thick, heavy glass. They are built to hold far more pressure than a bottle of still wine ever faces.
The amount of gas is remarkable. It is often described as five to six times the bottle's own volume of carbon dioxide, measured at ordinary pressure.
In the early days, winemakers had no reliable way to measure how much sugar a wine held, so the pressure a bottle would build was largely a matter of guesswork.
Too much sugar meant too much gas, and bottles burst in the cellars. One bottle breaking could shake its neighbours, so losses could spread along a rack.
How many were lost is hard to pin down. Old accounts give figures from a few per cent to most of a cellar, so we would rather not choose between them.
Two changes helped. Glass became stronger, helped by the coal-fired furnaces of English glassmakers, so bottles could better withstand the pressure inside them.
The second change was measurement. In the 1830s a pharmacist in Châlons-sur-Marne set out a way to gauge a wine's sugar before bottling, so the dose could be calculated.
Accounts describe breakage falling sharply as his method spread, though it was imprecise, and the measurement was refined for many years afterwards.
Today the dose is measured with care and the glass is strong, so the danger that once shaped the cellars has largely been tamed.
When the prise de mousse ends, the yeast has done its work and dies, settling as a fine sediment called the lees. The wine is now dry and sparkling.
You might expect the story to end there, yet its most patient chapter is only beginning, and those spent yeast cells are its quiet heroes.
episodes.setup: The bubbles are made, yet the champagne is far from ready. Next, we discover why the rules insist on a long, patient wait in the dark.

episodes.title: Waiting on the Lees
episodes.hook: Once the bubbles have formed, champagne could in principle be finished within weeks. Instead the rules make it wait, and the best producers wait far longer, because of what the spent yeast slowly gives back to the wine.
episodes.callback: We saw the prise de mousse fill the sealed bottle with pressure and leave a fine sediment of yeast behind.
cards: The sediment left by the second fermentation is called the lees, from the French lies. It is made of yeast cells that have finished their work.
Rather than removing it at once, the Champenois leave the wine lying on its lees, sometimes for many years, in the cool and steady dark of the cellar.
Slowly, the yeast cells break down from within, through their own enzymes. This gentle self-digestion is called autolysis, and it is the reason for the wait.
As they break down, the cells release substances into the wine, among them amino acids, proteins, and sugars bound to proteins, which are called mannoproteins.
Mannoproteins are often credited with a smoother, creamier texture, while amino acids and fats from the yeast feed the slow development of aroma.
This is where the flavours often described as bread, brioche, biscuit and toast come from, the qualities that many people treasure most in an older champagne.
The lees also help to protect the wine. They take up oxygen inside the bottle, which keeps the wine fresh while all this slow change unfolds.
Autolysis does not hurry. The Oxford Companion to Wine describes its effects as minimal with under eighteen months on the lees, and greatest after about five years.
Because the change is so slow, the rules of the Champagne appellation set minimum times, so that no champagne reaches you before it has had at least some of it.
For a non-vintage champagne, at least fifteen months must pass between the tirage, the bottling for the second fermentation, and the moment the wine is released.
For a vintage champagne the minimum is thirty-six months, again counted from the date of tirage. That is the three years you will often see quoted.
The rules also hold back disgorgement, the removal of the yeast, until at least twelve months after tirage, so every champagne spends a year or more on its lees.
Put together, a non-vintage champagne may lose its yeast after a year, but the full fifteen months from tirage must have passed before it may be sold.
In practice the wait is usually longer. The region's own body says non-vintage champagnes typically spend two to three years in the cellar, and vintage ones four to ten.
Some prestige wines rest on their lees for well over a decade, and producers occasionally release older bottles that have waited longer still.
Time on the lees is a choice of style as well as patience. Longer is not always better for every wine, and producers weigh freshness against richness.
Many producers now print the disgorgement date on the back label, so you can tell how long the wine has rested since its yeast was removed.
Champagne changes after the yeast is gone too, in a slower and different way, which we will return to when the bottle receives its final cork.
All this waiting creates a puzzle of its own. The lees must eventually leave the bottle, without the wine and the pressure leaving with them.
Lying on its side, the sediment has spread along the glass. The next problem the cellar had to solve was how to gather it neatly in one place.
episodes.setup: The yeast has given all it can, and now it must go. Next comes the patient business of gathering it up and sending it out of the bottle.

episodes.title: Turning and Clearing
episodes.hook: Early sparkling champagne could be hazy with yeast, and removing it cleanly took real ingenuity. The answer came in two parts: first gather the sediment in the neck, then let the bottle's own pressure push it out.
episodes.callback: We left the bottles resting on their lees while the yeast quietly gave the wine its depth.
cards: To remove the lees, they first have to be moved. Coaxing the sediment down into the neck of the bottle is called remuage, or riddling in English.
The classic tool is the pupitre, two heavy wooden boards hinged at the top like a letter A, each pierced with angled holes that hold bottles by the neck.
A classic pupitre holds one hundred and twenty bottles, sixty on each side, in ten rows of six slanting holes.
Day after day, a skilled riddler, the remueur, gives each bottle a small twist and a gentle jolt, and gradually tips it from lying flat towards standing upside down.
Bit by bit, the sediment slides down the glass and gathers against the closure. By hand this takes weeks; sources range from about six weeks to a few months.
The method is closely tied to the house of Veuve Clicquot, and to Barbe-Nicole Clicquot, the widow who ran it in the early nineteenth century.
The story goes that, around 1816, she had holes cut at an angle into a table, so that bottles could stand neck down and their sediment settle against the cork.
It is easy to see why the story is loved: a young widow at the head of a wine house, solving a stubborn problem at her own kitchen table.
The history is more shared. The Union des Maisons de Champagne tells it as a story in which an employee, Antoine Müller, her cellar master, prompted the idea.
Sources also differ on the year, offering dates from about 1816 to 1818, and some writers treat the kitchen table itself as legend rather than record.
What seems fair is to credit the Clicquot cellar, the widow and her cellar master together, with an idea that others refined. The pupitre as we know it came later.
Riddling by hand is skilled and slow work, and in the twentieth century inventors looked for a machine that could copy the remueur's movements.
The answer was the gyropalette, a metal cage holding several hundred bottles at once, which tilts and turns them all together on a programmed rhythm.
Its inventors, two French growers, filed their patent in 1968. Sources differ on when it was first sold and when it caught on, placing both within the 1970s.
A gyropalette can finish its work in about a week, running day and night. Most champagne is riddled this way today, though some is still riddled by hand.
Once the sediment rests in the neck, the bottles can be stored upside down until the moment of dégorgement, or disgorgement, the removal of the yeast.
The older method is dégorgement à la volée, on the fly. The bottle is opened by hand, and its pressure throws out the sediment with a little of the wine.
Done well, it is quick and deft, with the bottle angled and the opening covered at once. It is still used for some prestige wines and large bottles.
In the nineteenth century a method arrived that freezes the neck first. The neck is dipped into a very cold brine, and the sediment becomes a small icy plug.
When the cap comes off, the pressure pushes out the frozen plug cleanly, losing very little wine or gas. Sources commonly date the method to the 1880s.
This is dégorgement à la glace, and today it is the most widely used method. What remains in the bottle is clear, sparkling and usually very dry.
episodes.setup: The bottle is clear, dry and a little short of wine. Next, we see how a small measure of liqueur, a cork and a wire cage complete it.

episodes.title: The Final Touch
episodes.hook: After all those months of waiting, the last steps happen in moments. A small measure of liquid is added, a cork goes in, and a wire cage holds it fast against the pressure inside.
episodes.callback: We watched the sediment walk down into the neck and leave the bottle as a small frozen plug.
cards: Disgorgement leaves the bottle a little short of wine, and the wine itself is usually very dry. Both are addressed in one gesture, called the dosage.
The dosage is a small amount of liquid called the liqueur d'expédition, the shipping liqueur, named for the moment the wine is made ready to leave the cellar.
It is usually wine with sugar dissolved in it, often cane or beet sugar, though some producers use concentrated grape must instead.
Many cellars prepare their liqueur d'expédition well in advance, from carefully chosen wines, because this small addition will be part of every glass poured.
Dosage exists to answer acidity. A wine from a cool climate, after its years on the lees, can taste austere, and a little sugar can bring it into balance.
Done well, it works more like seasoning than sweetening. The sugar rounds the edges and lifts the fruit long before you would notice it as sweetness.
How much a producer adds is a question of style, and the label names the category, from wines with no added sugar at all to the sweet ones served with dessert.
Some producers prefer to add nothing, letting ripeness and long ageing provide the balance. Others feel a measured dosage shows their wine at its best. Both are honest choices.
The dosage also shapes how a champagne ages after disgorgement. Sugars and the amino acids left by the lees can react slowly together, in what chemists call the Maillard reaction.
That slow reaction is thought to bring toasty, nutty and caramel notes over time. Researchers are still asking whether dosage sugar or the wine's own sugar matters more.
Once the dosage is in, the bottle receives its final closure. A champagne cork usually has a body of bonded cork granules, faced with one or more discs of natural cork.
The disc that touches the wine is called the mirror. Before it goes in, the cork is a straight cylinder about thirty-one millimetres across, far wider than the neck.
It is squeezed hard to enter the bottle, and only part of it goes in. The top that remains outside is pressed into the familiar mushroom shape.
A cork alone could not be trusted against so much pressure, so a wire cage holds it down. The French call it a muselet, from museler, to muzzle.
Under the wire sits a small metal cap, the plaque, which stops the wire from biting into the cork. Collectors now seek out these decorated little caps.
A patent filed in 1844 by Adolphe Jacquesson is often linked to the muselet, though sources disagree on whether it covered the wire itself or the protective plaque.
Traditionally the wire loop opens with six half-turns, though some guides count the turns differently, so think of the number as a pleasant custom rather than a rule.
Once you pour, a little more science comes into view. Research has found that most bubbles do not form on the glass itself, but on tiny fibres resting on it.
These hollow fibres of cellulose, left by the air or a drying cloth, trap a pocket of gas, which swells with carbon dioxide from the wine until a bubble breaks free.
A glass made perfectly smooth and clean, with no fibres or scratches, would hardly bubble at all, which is why some glasses carry tiny etched marks in the bowl.
After corking, the bottle usually rests a while longer, so the dosage can settle into the wine, and then at last it is ready to leave the cellar.
episodes.setup: Every step so far has served a pale champagne. Next, we look at the two ways the Champenois let a little colour in, and the rule that makes one of them unusual.

episodes.title: Pink Champagne
episodes.hook: Rosé champagne can be made in two quite different ways. One of them, blending a little red wine into white, is something European rules do not allow for ordinary still rosé, and it is worth understanding why Champagne may do it.
episodes.callback: We closed the bottle with its cork and muselet and followed the bubbles into the glass.
cards: Pink champagne, rosé, follows almost every step we have described so far. The difference lies at the very beginning, in how the wine gets its colour.
The colour of black grapes sits in their skins. A white champagne keeps juice and skins apart, while a rosé lets a little of that colour through, on purpose.
There are two ways to do it. The first, and the most common in Champagne, is to blend a small amount of still red wine into the white base wine.
This is called rosé d'assemblage, rosé by blending. The red wine is made from Champagne's own black grapes, Pinot Noir or Meunier, or both.
The blending happens before the second fermentation, during assemblage, so the red wine joins the blend and then sparkles along with everything else.
Producers value this method for its control. The colour, and some of the flavour, can be adjusted precisely and kept consistent from one year to the next.
Here Champagne stands apart. European Union rules do not allow an ordinary still rosé to be made by mixing red and white wine together.
The same rules make an exception for wine being blended to become a sparkling wine, and Champagne is the best-known place where that allowance is used.
So the blended rosé is not a shortcut that has slipped past the law. It is an allowance made for sparkling wine, and Champagne has made it very much its own.
In 2009 a proposal to loosen the rule for still wines was debated, and producers of traditional rosé argued firmly against it. The plan was dropped.
The second method takes colour straight from the skins. Black grapes are left in contact with their juice for a short time, until it reaches the shade the winemaker wants.
In Champagne this is called rosé de saignée or rosé de macération. Saignée means bleeding, a picture of the coloured juice being drawn off the skins.
Timing is everything. Too short a contact and the colour is faint; too long and the wine grows deeper and more tannic, so each year's grapes must be judged afresh.
Wines made this way are often deeper in colour and fuller in flavour, and their shade can vary more between years, because the grapes alone decide it.
A number of houses and growers choose this method for some or all of their rosés. Drappier, in the Côte des Bar, makes each of its rosés by saignée.
Neither method is better in itself. Blending is simpler and more repeatable, while maceration lets the grapes set the colour. Each answers a different idea of rosé.
Whichever route they take, rosé champagnes then pass through the same second fermentation, time on the lees, riddling, disgorgement and dosage as any other.
You may also meet Rosé des Riceys, a still pink wine from Les Riceys in the south of the region. It has its own appellation and is not a champagne.
So the pink in your glass is a small decision made right at the start, and carried patiently through every step that follows.
episodes.setup: That completes the journey from grape to glass. Last of all comes our scorecard: what has held, what has changed, and what we chose to leave out.

episodes.title: Scorecard
episodes.hook: Every thread here ends with an honest account. This is where we gather what has held up, what has changed over time, the popular versions we have gently corrected, and what we chose to leave out, with our reasons.
episodes.callback: We saw rosé take its colour in two ways, from a little red wine in the blend or from a short time on the skins.
cards: First, what has held. Champagne is still made twice, first as a still wine and then, inside its own bottle, as a sparkling one. Every later step serves that idea.
Picking by hand and pressing whole bunches still answer the same old problem: drawing pale juice from black grapes without letting their colour escape.
The pressing limits stand at 2,550 litres from each 4,000-kilo marc, divided into 2,050 litres of cuvée and 500 litres of taille.
The minimum times still count from tirage: fifteen months before release for non-vintage, thirty-six for vintage, and at least twelve before disgorgement.
Next, what has changed. The pressing rules were once more generous; sources describe a larger total, and a further pressing that may no longer become champagne.
Riddling has largely moved from the pupitre to the gyropalette, and disgorgement from the hand to the frozen neck, though both older skills survive for special bottles.
Some producers have gone back to sealing with cork for the second fermentation, a reminder that older ways are sometimes chosen again on purpose.
Some popular versions deserve a gentle correction. The bubbles are not pumped in; they come from the yeast, inside the bottle, during the prise de mousse.
Madame Clicquot is often given sole credit for the riddling table. Her cellar master, Antoine Müller, belongs in the story too, and the kitchen table may be legend.
Méthode champenoise is still a familiar phrase. In the European Union, wines from outside Champagne have not been able to use it on labels since the 1990s.
Those wines say méthode traditionnelle, or a local version such as metodo classico, for the same method of a second fermentation in the bottle.
And rosé champagne is not a loophole. European rules forbid blending red and white for ordinary still rosé, and allow it for wines that are destined to sparkle.
Finally, what we left out, and why. We gave no figure for how many bottles once burst in the cellars, because old accounts range from a few per cent to most of a cellar.
We did not name the pharmacist who first measured sugar for the tirage, because our sources gave him different first names, although they agree on Châlons and the 1830s.
We gave the gyropalette's patent year, 1968, but no single date for its arrival in the cellars, because sources place its first sales at different points in the 1970s.
We gave no share of reserve wine for any blend, since it varies so much between producers and years that any single number would mislead.
We did not say when crown caps replaced corks for the second fermentation, because we could not find a source that settled the date.
We also kept Dom Pérignon out of this account. The stories about him are many, and they deserve a careful telling of their own.
Thank you for following the bottle all the way from the vineyard to the glass. We hope your next champagne feels a little like a story you already know.
